chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: The history of Mali can be divided into several major periods: Pre-Imperial Mali (before the 13th century) The Mali Empire (13th–17th centuries) The  Songhai Empire (15th–16th centuries) The borders of Mali are those of French Sudan, drawn in 1891. They unite part of the larger Sudan region with parts of the Sahara.

events.label: 9500 BC
events.text: During this period, which began around 9500 BCE, the landscape of northern Mali resembled the savannah ecosystems found in southern Mali today.

events.label: 9400 BC
events.text: Pottery appeared independently at several sites, including Ounjougou in central Mali, with ceramics dated to around 9400 BCE – one of the earliest known examples in West Africa.

events.label: 8000 BC
events.text: Sorghum and millet were among the earliest cultivated crops, and by 8000 BCE, large herds of cattle – closely related to modern zebus – grazed across what is now the Sahara.

events.label: 5000 BC
events.text: The humid phase that followed the Younger Dryas (a cold climatic episode) was eventually replaced by increasing aridity around 5000 BCE.

events.label: 4000 BC
events.text: Archaeological and paleoenvironmental data suggest a return of nomadic pastoralists around 4000 BCE, just prior to the end of the last humid phase, which waned around 3500 BCE.

events.label: 250 BC
events.text: Another major site was Djenné-Djenno, occupied from approximately 250 BCE to 800 CE.

Beginning in 1230, the Mali Empire was the largest empire in West Africa and profoundly influenced the culture of the region through the spread of its language, laws, and customs along the Niger River.
After Soumaoro Kanté's defeat in the Battle of Kirina in 1235, the Ghana Empire became permanent allies with the Mali Empire.

events.label: 13th c.
events.text: The history of Mali can be divided into several major periods: Pre-Imperial Mali (before the 13th century) The Mali Empire (13th–17th centuries) The  Songhai Empire (15th–16th centuries) The borders of Mali are those of French Sudan, drawn in 1891.

events.label: 19th c.
events.text: Until the 19th century, the city of Timbuktu remained important as an outpost at the southwestern fringe of the Muslim world and a hub of the trans-Saharan slave trade.

chapters.narrative: The history of Mali can be divided into several major periods: Pre-Imperial Mali before the 13th century, the Mali Empire from the 13th to 17th centuries, and the Songhai Empire in the 15th to 16th centuries [S1]. The borders of Mali are those of French Sudan, drawn in 1891, which unite part of the larger Sudan region with parts of the Sahara [S1]. Beginning in 1230, the Mali Empire was the largest empire in West Africa and profoundly influenced the culture of the region through the spread of its language, laws, and customs along the Niger River [S1]. After Soumaoro Kanté's defeat in the Battle of Kirina in 1235, the Ghana Empire became permanent allies with the Mali Empire [S1].

chapters.title: After the empires (1591–1892)
chapters.summary: The Songhai empire eventually collapsed under pressure from the Moroccan Saadi dynasty. The turning point was the Battle of Tondibi of March 13, 1591.

events.text: The turning point was the Battle of Tondibi of March 13, 1591.

events.label: 17th c.
events.text: The Senufo Kenedugu Kingdom originated in the 17th century in the area around what is now the border of Mali and Burkina Faso.
The Bambara Empire existed as a centralized state from 1712 to 1861.
A split in the Coulibaly dynasty in Ségou led to the establishment of a second Bambara state, the kingdom of Kaarta, in what is now western Mali, in 1753.
It was defeated in 1854 by Umar Tall, leader of Toucouleur Empire, before his war with Ségou.
Umar Tall's mujahideen readily defeated the Bambara, seizing Ségou itself on March 10, 1861, and declaring an end to the empire.
It later allied with Bambara Empire against Umar Tall's Toucouleur Empire and was also defeated by it in 1862.
This empire, founded by El Hadj Umar Tall of the Toucouleur peoples, beginning in 1864, ruled eventually most of what is now Mali until the French conquest of the region in 1890.
The Wassoulou or Wassulu Empire was a short-lived (1878–1898) empire, led by Samori Ture in the predominantly Malinké area of what is now upper Guinea and southwestern Mali (Wassoulou).
It resisted the effort of Samori Ture, leader of Wassoulou Empire, in 1887, to conquer it, and was one of the last kingdoms in the area to fall to the French in 1898.

chapters.narrative: The Songhai empire collapsed under pressure from the Moroccan Saadi dynasty with the Battle of Tondibi of March 13, 1591 as the turning point [S2]. The Senufo Kenedugu Kingdom originated in the 17th century around what is now the border of Mali and Burkina Faso [S2]. The Bambara Empire existed as a centralized state from 1712 to 1861, and a split in the Coulibaly dynasty led to the kingdom of Kaarta in what is now western Mali in 1753 [S2]. Umar Tall's mujahideen seized Ségou on March 10, 1861 [S2]. The Toucouleur Empire founded by El Hadj Umar Tall beginning in 1864 ruled most of what is now Mali until the French conquest in 1890 [S2].

chapters.title: French Sudan (1892–1960)
chapters.summary: Mali fell under French colonial rule in 1892. By 1893, the French appointed a civilian governor of the territory they called Soudan Français (French Sudan), but active resistance to French rule continued.

events.text: Mali fell under French colonial rule in 1892.
By 1893, the French appointed a civilian governor of the territory they called Soudan Français (French Sudan), but active resistance to French rule continued.
By 1905, most of the area was under firm French control.
In 1958 the renamed Sudanese Republic obtained complete internal autonomy and joined the French Community.
On June 20, 1960, the Federation of Mali became an independent country and Modibo Keïta became its first President.

chapters.narrative: Mali fell under French colonial rule in 1892 [S3]. By 1893, the French appointed a civilian governor of the territory they called Soudan Français (French Sudan), but active resistance to French rule continued [S3]. By 1905, most of the area was under firm French control [S3]. In 1958 the renamed Sudanese Republic obtained complete internal autonomy and joined the French Community [S3]. On June 20, 1960, the Federation of Mali became an independent country and Modibo Keïta became its first President [S3]. The excerpts only reflect a French colonial administrative point of view as presented [S3].

chapters.title: Independence (1960–present)
chapters.summary: Following the withdrawal of Senegal from the federation in August 1960, the former Sudanese Republic became the Republic of Mali on September 22, 1960, with Modibo Keïta as president. President Modibo Keïta, whose Sudanese Union-African Democratic Rally (US/RDA) party had dominated pre-independence politics (as a member of the African Democratic Rally), moved quickly to declare a single-party state and to pursue a socialist policy based on extensive nationalization.

A new constitution, approved in 1974, created a one-party state and was designed to move Mali toward civilian rule.
In September 1976, a new political party was established, the Democratic Union of the Malian People (UDPM), based on the concept of democratic centralism.

In National Assembly elections in June 1988, multiple UDPM candidates were permitted to contest each seat, and the regime organized nationwide conferences to consider how to implement democracy within the one-party framework.
By 1990, cohesive opposition movements began to emerge, including the National Democratic Initiative Committee and the Alliance for Democracy in Mali (Alliance pour la Démocratie au Mali, ADEMA).

The 2002 election was a milestone, marking Mali's first successful transition from one democratically elected president to another, despite the persistence of electoral irregularities and low voter turnout.
In August 2018, President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta was re-elected for a new five-year term after winning the second round of the election against Soumaïla Cissé.
On May 25, 2021, Colonel Assimi Goita dismissed the transitional president Bah N'Daw and the transitional prime minister Moctar Ouane from their positions.

chapters.narrative: Following the withdrawal of Senegal from the federation in August 1960, the former Sudanese Republic became the Republic of Mali on September 22, 1960, with Modibo Keïta as president [S4]. His Sudanese Union-African Democratic Rally party moved quickly to declare a single-party state and to pursue a socialist policy based on extensive nationalization [S4]. On November 19, 1968, a group of young officers staged a bloodless coup and set up a 14-member Military Committee for National Liberation (CMLN) [S4]. A new constitution, approved in 1974, created a one-party state and was designed to move Mali toward civilian rule [S4]. In September 1976, a new political party was established, the Democratic Union of the Malian People (UDPM), based on the concept of democratic centralism [S4].
